results.content: # PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. The PI3K/AKT, mTOR and PTEN pathways are interconnected cellular signaling components that regulate many cellular processes like growth, proliferation, survival, metabolism and more. ## The Harmony of Cellular Regulation: Exploring the PI3K/AKT/mTOR and PTEN Dynamics. Among the myriad of pathways involved in intracellular signaling, the PI3K/AKT, mTOR and PTEN pathways are particularly pivotal. The PI3K/AKT pathway is a vital communication route within cells, directing their responses based on signals from their surroundings. The PI3K/AKT pathway can become activated in response to various stimuli, particularly when growth factors bind to their specific receptors on a cell's surface such as when insulin binds the insulin receptor to affect glucose metabolism. ## PTEN – The Guardian of the PI3K/AKT Pathway. PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) acts as a critical regulator, ensuring that the PI3K/AKT pathway's activities are kept in check. PTEN's inhibition of the PI3K/AKT pathway is pivotal for controlling cell growth and survival. Beyond its central role in the PI3K/AKT pathway, PTEN interacts with and influences other pathways, including the MAPK/ERK pathway and the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Activation signals from the PI3K/AKT pathway, such as those triggered by insulin or other growth factors, play a significant role in modulating mTOR's activity. However, signals from the PI3K/AKT pathway can inhibit the TSC1/2 complex, leading to mTORC1 activation. Though not as well-understood, mTORC2 plays roles in controlling the actin cytoskeleton and is crucial for the full activation of AKT, linking it to the broader PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. The PI3K/AKT pathway directly influences mTOR, especially mTORC1. AKT can promote mTORC1 activity, leading to increased protein synthesis and cell growth. Conversely, PTEN, by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT pathway, can indirectly suppress mTOR activity, emphasizing the interconnectedness of these pathways. The PI3K/AKT, mTOR, and PTEN pathways are integral to human health, influencing a range of diseases, especially cancer. Dysregulation, such as overactivation of the PI3K/AKT pathway due to PTEN dysfunction, can drive tumor growth and resistance to therapies. results.title: Akt/mTOR Signaling - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Akt mTOR signaling refers to the interconnected signaling pathways involving the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) and Akt, which play crucial roles in regulating cell survival, proliferation, and metabolism in response to growth factors and cellular stress. PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling plays a key role in CSC biology because this pathway is more sensitive to inhibition compared to healthy stem cells [191,207]. As such, small molecule inhibitors targeting major kinase components of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway have drawn extensive attention and been developed and evaluated in preclinical models and clinical trials. We hope that this review will facilitate further understanding of the regulatory mechanisms governing dysregulation of PI3K/Akt/mTOR oncogenic signaling in cancer and provide insights into possible future directions for targeted therapeutic regimen for cancer treatment, by developing new agents, drug delivery systems, or combination regimen to target the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway. The PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway is one of the most frequently dysregulated networks in human cancer, which is involved in the development and progression of both solid and blood tumors through modulating either intrinsic cellular programs, including tumor cell proliferation, growth and metastasis, or regulating tumor microenvironment, including angiogenesis, inflammation, immune responses and others. Given that this is an intra-cellular oncogenic kinase signaling, small molecule inhibitors targeting various kinase components of this signaling, including PI3K, Akt and mTOR, have been developed and evaluated in cancer cell lines, preclinical models and clinical trials. Since PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling is indispensable not only for cancer but also for normal healthy cells, it is not surprising that mono-therapies targeting PI3K, Akt, or mTOR does not achieve satisfactory clinical outcome due to common toxicity issues associated with adverse effects, as well as developed treatment resistance. Another direction is to identify cancer-specific activation mechanisms for PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling so that these new upstream regulators may serve as novel drug targets, upon inhibition of which specific inhibition of this signaling in cancer but not healthy cells could be achieved. Current PI3K/Akt/mTOR inhibitors largely target the catalytic kinase activity for inhibition and leave non-kinase function of this signaling unaffected. If other PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling components exert critical roles in tumorigenesis, and if this function is dysregulated in cancer, then if and how to target non-kinase oncogenic function for inhibition remain challenging questions to answer.
